title: From secants to the derivative
sub: The derivative is the limit of slopes, and it is a function in its own right.

frames.caption: f(x) = x². What is its slope at x = 2? A slope needs two points, so start with a second point h further along and draw the line through both (a secant).
h = 1: slope = (f(2 + h) − f(2)) / h = 5. Algebra says it's exactly 4 + h.
h = 0.5: slope = (f(2 + h) − f(2)) / h = 4.5. Shrink h: the second point slides toward the first and the line swings.
h = 0.25: slope = (f(2 + h) − f(2)) / h = 4.25. Shrink h: the second point slides toward the first and the line swings.
h = 0.1: slope = (f(2 + h) − f(2)) / h = 4.1. Now the two points are almost on top of each other.
h = 0.01: slope = (f(2 + h) − f(2)) / h = 4.01. Now the two points are almost on top of each other.
As h → 0 the slope 4 + h → 4, and the secant becomes the tangent line (teal). That limit is the derivative: f′(2) = 4. You never set h = 0 (that would be 0/0); you ask where the slopes are heading.
f(x) = sin x. At every point it has a slope. Slide a tangent line along the curve and record each slope as a height (orange dots).
At the peak (x = π/2) the tangent is flat: slope 0, so the traced curve crosses zero here.
At x = π, sin is falling fastest: slope −1, the lowest point of the traced curve.
The slopes trace out a new function: cos x. That is what “the derivative is a function” means: f′(x) is the slope of f at every x, and for sin it is exactly cos.
